narrative_md:
**The UK is paying Mauritius around £3 billion over 99 years to lease back a military base Britain has occupied since 1968.**

On 3 October 2024, five days after the first Starmer-Jugnauth summit, the UK announced it would cede sovereignty of the Chagos Archipelago to Mauritius in exchange for a 99-year lease of Diego Garcia, the US-operated strategic base. Lifetime payments to Mauritius are expected to exceed £3 billion. The Conservatives, the Trump transition team, and several US senators all opposed the deal. The treaty was initialled in October 2024, modified by the new Mauritian government in early 2025, and signed in May 2025.

**The legal backdrop is 60 years old.** Britain excised the Chagos Archipelago from Mauritius in 1965, three years before Mauritian independence, creating the British Indian Ocean Territory. Between 1968 and 1973 the entire Chagossian population — roughly 1,500 people — was forcibly removed, predominantly to Mauritius and Seychelles. Diego Garcia was leased to the United States which built a major naval and strategic air base; it has hosted B-52s, nuclear submarines, and reportedly CIA rendition flights post-2001. In 2019 the ICJ issued an advisory opinion that UK sovereignty was unlawful; the UN General Assembly voted 116-6 for Chagos to return to Mauritius. Britain refused.

**The negotiation.** Under Truss, Cleverly and Cameron (as Foreign Secretaries), 11 rounds of talks were held 2022-24. Labour inherited the file. Foreign Secretary David Lammy and Attorney General Richard Hermer decided — controversially — that continued UK occupation without resolution risked a binding ICJ judgment and jeopardised US base operations in a future legal squeeze. The 3 October 2024 announcement said sovereignty would transfer to Mauritius; Britain would lease Diego Garcia for 99 years; resettlement of Chagossians to the outer islands (not Diego Garcia) would be permitted; and a 'substantial' financial package would flow to Mauritius.

**The money.** The Government did not publish the lifetime cost in October 2024, which enraged the PAC and the Lords Joint Committee on Human Rights. The Treasury estimate eventually disclosed in 2025 — around £3.4bn net present value over 99 years — includes annual lease payments, a development fund for Mauritius, and a Chagossian Trust Fund. Per-year cost: roughly £100m, adjusted for inflation. That is comparable in order of magnitude to the UK's NATO-above-2% uplift per year.

**The political opposition.** Kemi Badenoch (then Business Secretary, from November 2024 Conservative leader) called the deal 'a betrayal'. Trump, via Rubio and Waltz, said in January 2025 he would review — though the base itself is protected by the lease. The Mauritian election of November 2024 brought Navin Ramgoolam's Labour Party back to power, and his government demanded renegotiation of the financial terms — a larger upfront payment, shorter lease. Terms were re-settled in March-April 2025 and signed May 2025.

**The Chagossians are mostly excluded.** Resettlement to Diego Garcia itself is not permitted under the treaty — the strategic base is off-limits. The outer Salomon and Peros Banhos groups, where palm plantations operated before 1971, are available. Chagossian diaspora communities in Crawley (UK), Mauritius and Seychelles are divided: some welcome sovereignty return; others, organised via Chagossian Voices and UK-based activists, say the UK and Mauritius negotiated over their heads.

**The strategic logic.** Diego Garcia's runway, harbour and communications are central to US Indo-Pacific posture. Securing the base under a treaty with a friendly Commonwealth state — rather than contested sovereignty — reduces legal risk to the US operational footprint. Whether £3bn is the right price, and whether the deal survives future Mauritian governments, are open questions. The decolonisation logic — unfinished Empire business returning to haunt the 21st-century Treasury — is the thread that ties it to every other late-colonial financial settlement still working through British accounts.
